claim: Paleontological FEA is an end-to-end model of geometry, materials, loads and constraints, not merely a solver choice.
Geometry, density/material properties and segmentation-related uncertainty can be treated as distinct CT-to-FEA input uncertainties.
Different mesh-generation methods can trade accuracy, human effort and computational cost differently.
Surface smoothing can reduce numerical surface stress oscillation in CT-derived FE models, while modifying the geometry.
Mesh refinement addresses discretization uncertainty; it does not by itself establish physical validity.
Cranial strain and displacement responses can vary with mesh density, and different regions can converge at different rates.
Cranial FE models can match loading conditions while still missing some local measured strain magnitudes.
Geometry/segmentation simplifications can leave global deformation modes comparatively stable while altering localized strain magnitudes.
Human cranial FE validation found absolute deformations were not accurately predicted, while global strain-pattern distributions were more reasonably approximated.
Surface-mesh resolution is a distinct sensitivity layer from solid-mesh resolution.
Digital fossil repair/restoration operations introduce interpretive uncertainty that can propagate into functional analyses.
A watertight, closed, non-manifold-free and non-self-intersecting surface is a prerequisite for reliable tetrahedralization in the cited fossil workflow.
Deep-learning segmentation can greatly reduce manual effort, but CT artifacts, low fossil-matrix contrast and rapid anatomical changes remain failure modes.
In a Jeholosaurus femur, removing matrix from intertrabecular spaces changed stress magnitudes and spatial correspondence with trabecular structure.
Adjacent biomechanics literature can quantify FE output sensitivity to segmentation differences rather than treating segmentation as purely qualitative preprocessing.
Reporting guidance recommends stating the outputs used for mesh convergence, and whether they represent overall or regional responses.
Tetrahedral mesh quality depends strongly on boundary-surface quality and on the meshing algorithm; slivers and poor elements are recognized numerical risks.
Recent microFE evidence shows mesh type/resolution can have a stronger effect on local stress/strain than on global apparent stiffness.
